entries.answer:
Yes — the right shape is a server-side orchestrator that keeps durable session state, runs an explicit plan-execute-verify-adjust-retry loop, and streams progress over a long-lived SSE channel while coordinating parallel subagents for independent work branches.  The material also points toward a task-graph model with explicit merge points, rather than a stateless chat turn model, if you want real autonomy instead of sequential tool chaining.[1][2][3][4][5]

## Core loop

A useful internal representation is a task graph with source, transform, sink, and merge nodes, because that structure already appears in the local material and maps naturally onto planning, execution, synthesis, and final output.  The merge node matters most, because it gives you a first-class place to reunify parallel branches before verification and possible retry.  In practice, each node should carry status, inputs, outputs, evidence, attempt count, and a verifier result so every step can feed the next decision instead of vanishing into prompt history.[1]

## State

Long-running agent patterns in the gathered material emphasize explicit progress tracking and session continuity, including a persistent session progress file rather than ephemeral in-memory state.  The local kernel code shows the same idea in a more systems-oriented form: it keeps storage, a scheduler, access-flow analysis, cores, cycle counters, and migration counts on the server side, which is exactly the kind of durable control plane an autonomous agent needs.  The scheduler model also separates pending, active, and completed tasks, which is a strong template for agent work items and retries.[6][4]

| Component | Evidence from material | What to persist |
|---|---|---|
| Session record | Session continuity is treated as structured progress state. [4] | Session id, objective, plan version, cancellation flag, last event id |
| Work queue | Tasks are tracked as pending, active, and completed. [6] | Node status, retries, assigned worker, timestamps, outputs |
| Parallel branches | Parallel subagents run independent subtasks at the same time, and the local graph unit later synchronizes distributed work. [3][2] | Parent-child lineage, branch summaries, verifier verdicts |
| Resume control | Cancellation is proposed as session state checked by execution and streaming loops. [7] | Cancelled flag, checkpoint cursor, replay position |

A particularly important pattern is to store cancellation inside the session state and have both the execution loop and the streaming loop check it periodically.  That gives you safe stops, resumability, and retry without corrupting the rest of the run.[7]

## Streaming

For transport, use a long-lived SSE stream because A2A explicitly frames SSE as the mechanism for incremental results and ongoing status updates in long-running agent tasks.  The same source also recommends asynchronous notifications such as webhooks when clients cannot stay connected for very long jobs, which means your session must live on the server independently of any one connection.  A good event vocabulary is token, tool_use, thinking, progress, and done, because that exact pattern already appears in an agent-focused SSE protocol example.[8][5]

On top of that, add a heartbeat event every few seconds, include a monotonically increasing event id, and support replay from the last acknowledged cursor after reconnect. That makes the stream observable for humans, resumable for clients, and safe for multi-minute or multi-hour runs. It also lets you surface intermediate verification failures without tearing down the whole task.

## Parallelism

The clearest parallel pattern in the gathered material is a coordinator that launches multiple independent subagents at once instead of waiting for each subtask sequentially.  It is also worth noticing that some current agent environments still do not run sub-agents in parallel, which is a reminder that genuine autonomy requires deliberate orchestration rather than assuming the framework already provides it.  The local distributed-processing example reinforces the same lesson: it distributes a graph across active cores, processes matching in parallel, and then synchronizes local results back into a global graph.[2][3][9]

A second local example adds the operational side of autonomy by tracking data affinity, access patterns, cycle counts, migration, and periodic load balancing across cores.  That is a good blueprint for research agents too: fan out by question or hypothesis, keep branch-local state, then rebalance or retry only the weak branches instead of rerunning the entire plan. In other words, autonomy comes from explicit orchestration, durable memory, and verifier-driven control flow rather than from simply calling more tools.[6]

Would you like this turned into a concrete API and state-schema spec?

entries.query: Your task is to take the provided plan and rewrite it as a single, comprehensive prompt. Write it as if you were about to update the entire upgrade from the current state of the implementation: describe step by step, from beginning to end, exactly what you will construct and how you will construct it. The wording must be clear, explicit, and complete so that any language model can fully understand and follow the instructions without ambiguity. Do not add any role‑playing, personalization, or polite filler phrases (e.g., ‘You are a software developer’, ‘As an expert’, ‘Please kindly’). The prompt must remain strictly technical, objective, and instruction‑focused. Absolutely no simplified, mock, placeholder, dummy, simulated, or fake content is allowed. You must require the full ugrade  in complete, unabridged, production‑ready codes. Define what you want & what success looks like: “I want to [TASK] so that [SUCCESS CRITERIA].” No roles, “act as a senior expert.” That era is over.
entries.answer:
```text
I want to upgrade the current implementation into a durable, autonomous agent-orchestration runtime so that a submitted objective can be planned, decomposed, executed through tools and parallel subagents, continuously verified, retried or replanned when necessary, resumed after interruption, and observed in real time through reliable long-lived SSE streams.

Inspect the existing repository before changing code. Preserve all currently working behavior, public interfaces, data invariants, storage semantics, scheduling semantics, graph semantics, tests, and build configuration unless a change is required for this upgrade. Extend the implementation rather than replacing functioning subsystems with a simplified alternative. Produce the complete upgrade as unabridged, production-ready source code and tests. Do not produce pseudocode, placeholders, mock implementations, dummy data, stubs, simulated tool results, omitted sections, or incomplete files.

Build the upgrade around a durable server-side session model. Define a session as the authoritative lifecycle container for one user objective. Persist all session state outside the process memory so that a process restart, client disconnect, or worker restart does not destroy active work. Each session must have a unique immutable identifier; creation, update, checkpoint, completion, failure, cancellation, and archival timestamps; a version number for optimistic concurrency; a user objective; normalized execution constraints; a status; a cancellation state; a plan revision number; a last-emitted SSE event sequence number; and a resumable execution cursor.

Define explicit session statuses: queued, planning, executing, verifying, retrying, waiting_for_input, cancelling, cancelled, succeeded, failed, expired, and archived. Define valid state transitions and reject invalid transitions atomically. Never permit a terminal session to return to a non-terminal state unless an explicit clone-or-reopen operation creates a new session revision. Record every state transition as an append-only event with timestamp, actor, causal operation identifier, previous state, next state, and structured reason.

Represent work as a persistent directed acyclic task graph. A task node must contain a unique identifier, parent session identifier, optional parent task identifier, task kind, objective, inputs, dependency identifiers, execution status, priority, attempt count, retry budget, worker lease information, tool invocation information, result references, verifier result, failure classification, timestamps, and idempotency key. Support source nodes for user input, transform nodes for processing, tool nodes for external actions, verification nodes for acceptance checks, merge nodes for parallel-result synthesis, sink nodes for final outputs, and control nodes for replanning, cancellation, or human-input pauses. Preserve dependency ordering and do not execute a node until all required predecessors have succeeded or an explicit fallback policy permits continuation.

Use the existing data-flow graph concepts as the structural basis for plan decomposition and branch merging. A merge node must retain provenance for every incoming branch, including its source task identifier, evidence references, output digest, verifier verdict, elapsed time, retry count, and failure state. A synthesis operation must not silently discard failed or incomplete branches. It must expose branch-level outcomes to the verifier and include a deterministic policy for whether to continue, retry selected branches, replace failed branches, or fail the parent task.

Implement an agentic control loop with the following durable phases: intake, planning, dispatch, execution, observation, verification, adjustment, retry, replanning, synthesis, final verification, completion, and archival. Every phase must read the latest persisted session and task state, append auditable events, perform an idempotent state update, and write a checkpoint before releasing its worker lease. Do not treat model output as authoritative state. Parse model decisions into a typed action contract and validate that contract against the current session state, dependency graph, policy rules, retry limits, and tool schemas before acting on it.

During intake, validate the request, generate the session identifier, normalize input, establish budget limits, assign a default retry policy, create an initial source task, persist the session and task graph atomically, and emit a session_created event. During planning, create a typed plan containing milestones, task nodes, dependencies, expected evidence, verification criteria, success conditions, retry policies, required tools, and parallelism constraints. Require the plan to specify why each node exists, what artifact it produces, what verifier accepts it, and what failure condition triggers a retry or replan.

During dispatch, identify dependency-ready tasks, calculate priority, enforce per-session and global concurrency limits, acquire durable worker leases, and enqueue work without allowing duplicate active execution. Worker leases must include worker identifier, lease expiry, heartbeat timestamp, attempt identifier, and fencing token. A worker may update a task only when its fencing token matches the current task lease. Expired leases must be reclaimed safely, and reclaimed tasks must resume from the last completed checkpoint rather than beginning blindly from the start.

During execution, run tool calls and subagents through a strict orchestration layer. Every tool invocation must record a unique invocation identifier, immutable normalized input, timeout, retry policy, start time, end time, structured output reference, output digest, error class, and trace context. Enforce idempotency by reusing a prior completed invocation when the idempotency key, normalized request, and task revision match. Do not duplicate external side effects after a retry. For potentially non-idempotent tools, require an explicit compensation or confirmation strategy before execution.

Implement parallel research and sub-agent spawning. A parent task may create child tasks only through a validated spawn operation that records the parent-child relationship, subtask objective, allowed tools, budget, depth limit, expected artifact schema, verifier criteria, deadline, and cancellation inheritance. Permit independent child tasks to run concurrently when their inputs and side effects do not conflict. Enforce maximum fan-out, maximum nesting depth, session-level concurrency, global concurrency, per-tool concurrency, and resource budgets. Use independent branches for distinct research questions, source types, competing hypotheses, alternative execution strategies, or independent verification paths. Do not parallelize steps with unresolved data dependencies or shared mutable side effects unless the implementation provides locking and an explicit consistency policy.

Implement a scheduler that maintains pending, leased, active, blocked, retryable, completed, cancelled, and failed work states. Preserve task priority and fairness. Schedule tasks with awareness of dependency readiness, deadlines, historical duration, retry cost, available workers, tool quotas, and session budgets. Track pending, active, completed, failed, retried, cancelled, and timed-out task counts. Maintain queue latency, execution latency, verification latency, retry rate, task failure rate, and worker utilization metrics. Support periodic rebalancing without violating leases or task affinity.

Implement an evidence and memory layer. Store all meaningful task outputs, tool outputs, verifier reports, intermediate summaries, citations, structured facts, and final artifacts as immutable content-addressed records. Deduplicate identical content, preserve access metadata, attach provenance to every stored artifact, and maintain references from sessions, tasks, plans, tool invocations, and SSE events. Store metadata separately from raw payloads where practical. Retain high-value evidence using explicit relevance, novelty, recency, access frequency, and dependency-reference signals. Eviction must never remove an artifact reachable from an active session, incomplete task, active lease, verifier dependency, event log, or final result. Maintain integrity checks for object existence, digest consistency, reference validity, and lifecycle state.

Implement verification as a first-class control stage rather than a formatting step. Every task type must define its verification contract before execution begins. Verification must evaluate output schema validity, objective coverage, evidence completeness, tool-result consistency, dependency satisfaction, policy compliance, and task-specific acceptance conditions. A verifier must return one of accepted, rejected_retryable, rejected_replan_required, blocked_waiting_for_input, or failed_terminal. Persist the verifier report, including checks performed, evidence references, failure classification, recommended next action, and confidence or quality metrics where applicable.

When verification accepts a task, mark it completed and unblock dependent tasks. When verification returns rejected_retryable, increment the attempt count, compute bounded exponential backoff with jitter, persist a retry event, retain previous output and failure evidence, and retry only the smallest responsible task scope. When verification returns rejected_replan_required, generate a plan revision that preserves successful task outputs, invalidates only affected descendants, updates dependency edges, and emits an explicit replan event explaining the change. When verification returns blocked_waiting_for_input, transition the session to waiting_for_input, store the required question and context, stop dependent dispatch, and resume only after validated input is recorded. When verification returns failed_terminal, mark the appropriate task and session failure states with a structured failure report.

Implement retries with deterministic limits. Each task must have a maximum attempt count, maximum elapsed retry window, error-class allowlist, backoff policy, and escalation policy. Distinguish transient failures such as timeout, network interruption, worker loss, rate limit, and temporary external service failure from deterministic failures such as invalid input, schema mismatch, policy rejection, unavailable dependency, malformed tool contract, or exhausted budget. Do not retry deterministic failures unless the replan mechanism changes the preconditions. Include retry lineage in task state so the system can explain every attempt and reproduce the decision path.

Implement long-lived SSE streaming as a session-observation interface, not as the system of record. Provide an endpoint that subscribes to a session event stream using a session identifier and optional last event identifier. Persist all streamable events before publishing them. Assign strictly increasing sequence numbers per session. Support replay from the last acknowledged sequence number after client reconnect. Emit standard event types including session_created, session_state_changed, plan_created, plan_revised, task_created, task_leased, task_started, tool_started, tool_progress, tool_completed, tool_failed, subagent_spawned, subagent_completed, verification_started, verification_completed, retry_scheduled, replan_started, merge_started, merge_completed, artifact_created, heartbeat, warning, cancelled, failed, and completed.

Maintain a heartbeat mechanism at both connection and worker levels. For each SSE subscriber, send a heartbeat event at a configured interval even when no work events occur. For each worker lease, persist heartbeat updates at a configured interval and reclaim work only after a lease-expiry threshold that accounts for heartbeat freshness and clock tolerance. If an SSE connection drops, do not cancel the session; preserve execution server-side and allow replay on reconnection. If a client remains disconnected for a long-running session, continue processing and optionally deliver configured asynchronous completion notifications through a separate durable notification mechanism.

Implement SSE backpressure and recovery. Use bounded per-connection buffers. If a client cannot keep up, preserve the canonical event history server-side, terminate or resynchronize the slow connection predictably, and allow it to reconnect using the last received event identifier. Do not allow a slow client to block task execution or event persistence. Include event schema versioning and payload validation. Ensure terminal events are replayable and emitted exactly once in canonical event order, while delivery may be at-least-once and clients can deduplicate through sequence identifiers.

Implement cancellation and deadlines. Add a cancellation request operation that atomically marks a session as cancelling, emits an event, prevents new task dispatch, propagates cancellation to cancellable child tasks, and signals active workers through their persisted task state. Require workers, subagents, long-running tool adapters, and streaming loops to check cancellation at bounded intervals. Preserve partial results and event history after cancellation. Distinguish cancelled, cancellation_requested_but_not_confirmed, and cancellation_failed_due_to_noninterruptible_external_operation states. Support session deadlines, task deadlines, tool deadlines, and grace periods. On deadline breach, classify the result, cancel eligible descendants, and leave auditable evidence.

Define explicit APIs and complete request and response schemas for creating sessions, retrieving sessions, listing sessions, starting execution, receiving input for paused sessions, cancelling sessions, cloning sessions, retrieving plans, retrieving task graphs, retrieving task attempts, retrieving artifacts, retrieving event history, opening SSE streams, acknowledging stream cursors if used, and obtaining operational metrics. Validate all API input. Return stable machine-readable error codes and structured error payloads. Use pagination, filtering, and time-range query controls for event and artifact retrieval.

Implement authentication, authorization, tenancy boundaries, and audit logging for every session, task, artifact, and SSE subscription. Ensure one tenant cannot read, stream, modify, cancel, or infer the existence of another tenant’s session. Validate ownership before artifact retrieval, task retrieval, replay, cancellation, and resumed execution. Redact secrets from tool inputs, tool outputs, logs, SSE payloads, failure traces, and stored memory. Store secret references separately from plaintext values and prevent them from appearing in model context unless explicitly authorized and necessary.

Implement observability across the full lifecycle. Propagate trace identifiers from session creation through plan generation, task execution, tool invocations, subagent work, verification, retries, merge operations, storage operations, worker leases, and SSE delivery. Emit structured logs and metrics for state transitions, task outcomes, tool latency, external error rates, retries, lease reclamations, queue depth, stream connection count, replay count, heartbeat health, cancellation latency, and session completion outcomes. Add health and readiness checks that verify persistence connectivity, scheduler progress, worker availability, event append capability, artifact storage availability, and heartbeat freshness.

Implement crash recovery and server restart behavior. On startup, rebuild in-memory indexes only from durable state. Scan for sessions in non-terminal states, expire stale leases, requeue eligible tasks, detect incomplete tool invocations, preserve idempotency behavior, reconstruct scheduler queues, and resume SSE replay support from persisted event history. Verify that no task is concurrently active under two valid leases. Verify that all active sessions have reachable plans, all non-terminal tasks have valid parent sessions, all dependency references resolve, all artifact references exist, and all event sequences are contiguous per session.

Define and enforce invariants. A task cannot be completed without an accepted verifier result. A dependent task cannot start before required dependencies are accepted. A worker cannot write task results after losing its lease fencing token. A terminal task cannot become active again without a new attempt record. An event sequence number cannot be reused within a session. A persisted plan revision cannot contain cycles. A merge node cannot be accepted without recording the status of every required branch. An active session must remain recoverable from durable session, plan, task, artifact, and event records. An artifact referenced by a non-terminal workflow object cannot be evicted. A cancellation request must prevent future dispatch unless an explicit policy permits a non-cancellable cleanup task.

Add complete automated tests. Cover normal single-task completion; dependency ordering; plan creation; plan revision; parallel child-task execution; merge behavior; partial branch failure; verifier acceptance; verifier-triggered retry; verifier-triggered replan; retry budget exhaustion; transient tool failure; deterministic tool failure; tool idempotency; duplicate delivery; worker lease acquisition; worker heartbeat; stale lease reclamation; fencing-token rejection; process restart recovery; durable checkpoint recovery; cancellation before dispatch; cancellation during execution; deadline expiration; paused waiting-for-input flow; SSE connection; SSE heartbeat; SSE replay after reconnect; out-of-order or duplicate SSE delivery handling; slow-consumer behavior; event sequence continuity; authorization boundaries; artifact access control; secret redaction; storage deduplication; protected-artifact retention; scheduler fairness; concurrency limits; and metrics correctness.

Add integration tests that run an end-to-end session through planning, parallel research, tool execution, evidence storage, verification, retry or replan where appropriate, synthesis, final verification, SSE observation, reconnect replay, cancellation behavior, and final durable retrieval. The tests must use real implementations and deterministic local test adapters, not fake production paths. Include failure injection for persistence interruption, worker crash, lease expiry, tool timeout, SSE disconnect, duplicate invocation request, and server restart.

Update all repository documentation, configuration, migrations, API contracts, deployment instructions, operational runbooks, and environment-variable definitions required by the upgrade. Document schema migrations and backward compatibility. Include a safe migration path for existing state. Do not discard existing persisted data. Ensure the application starts cleanly with an empty environment, applies migrations safely, validates configuration at startup, exposes health checks, and fails fast with clear diagnostics when required dependencies are unavailable.

Success means that a user can submit one objective, disconnect immediately, reconnect later, replay every missed progress event, inspect the durable plan and task graph, observe multiple independent research branches running concurrently, see each tool result feed into verified next decisions, see failed work retried or replanned according to explicit policy, cancel safely, recover after a process restart, and retrieve a final result with complete provenance, verifier evidence, event history, and auditable state transitions.

Return the full upgrade as complete, unabridged, production-ready code for every modified or added file, together with all migrations, tests, configuration, and documentation required to build, run, verify, and deploy the implementation. Do not omit any file contents. Do not use placeholders, TODO markers, ellipses, mock logic, simulated behavior, or abbreviated snippets.
```
